name: sick
title: What Did Ancient Humans Do When They Got Sick? (They Did Surgery 31,000 Years Ago)

lines: Thirty-one thousand years ago, in a rainforest in Borneo, a child had part of their leg removed by surgery.
And the child survived. For years.
No hospitals. No metal tools. No idea that germs even existed.
So what did ancient humans actually do when they got sick?
Did they have medicine? Did they have doctors? Did anybody look after them?
The answer is cleverer, and kinder, than you might think.
Meet Moss. He has a sore tummy, a cut on his arm,
and a very bad case of feeling sorry for himself.
To see where medicine might have started, let's first visit our cousins.
In 1987, in the Mahale Mountains of Tanzania, scientists watched a sick chimpanzee do something odd.
She peeled the bark off a shrub, and slowly chewed the bitter pith inside.
Chimps hardly ever eat that plant. It tastes horrible.
But local people use the very same plant for tummy troubles and worms.
Within about a day, the chimp seemed to be feeling better.
Later tests found the plant contains chemicals that work against some of the worms chimps carry.
Then, in 2022, in Sumatra, an orangutan called Rakus hurt his face, probably in a fight.
So he chewed up a climbing plant, and smeared the juice right onto the wound.
Then he pressed the chewed plant on top. Like a little green plaster.
That plant is used in local medicine to fight swelling and germs.
Five days later, the wound had closed, with no sign of infection.
Scientists think it's the first time a wild animal has been seen treating a wound with a medicinal plant.
So if apes can do it, our ancestors probably could too.
Scientists think early medicine may have grown from the same instinct: try a plant, feel better, remember it, pass it on.
Remember the Neanderthal from our teeth video, who may have chewed poplar, a natural source of painkiller?
That fits the pattern.
But medicine isn't only about plants.
Sometimes, the medicine is people.
About fifty thousand years ago, in Shanidar Cave in Iraq, there lived a Neanderthal man.
Early in life, he took a terrible blow to the head.
He was probably blind in one eye. One arm was withered, and later lost at the elbow.
He walked with a limp. And scientists think he was very hard of hearing.
But all of those injuries had healed.
And he lived to around forty, or even older. That's old for a Neanderthal.
How do you hunt like that? Or hear a lion coming?
Scientists think the answer is simple. Other people helped him.
In a cave in Spain, scientists studied a tiny ear bone from a Neanderthal child they nicknamed Tina.
Its shape suggests Tina may have had Down syndrome, with poor hearing and bad dizzy spells.
Yet Tina lived to at least six years old.
Scientists think her mother couldn't have managed alone. The whole group probably pitched in.
So long before there were doctors, there were friends.
Being looked after may be one of the oldest medicines of all.
Which brings us back to Borneo.
In 2020, scientists digging in a cave called Liang Tebo found a skeleton.
It belonged to a young person, about nineteen or twenty years old.
And the lower part of their left leg was missing.
The bone ended neatly, and it had healed over smoothly.
Scientists think this wasn't an accident, or an animal attack. It was a planned operation.
From the way the bone grew, the surgery probably happened when they were a child.
They then lived for another six to nine years.
So how did they avoid a deadly infection?
Nobody knows for sure. But the scientists suggest rainforest plants with medicinal powers may have helped.
And this person lived in steep, rocky, jungle hills.
Getting around on one leg there would have needed a lot of help, for a lot of years.
When they died, they were buried with care, with stones placed over the grave.
Before this, the oldest known amputation was about seven thousand years old, from France.
Borneo pushed that back by twenty-four thousand years.
But there's an even stranger kind of Stone Age surgery.
And it involves the head.
It's called trepanation. Making a small hole in a living person's skull,
by slowly scraping or cutting through the bone with stone tools.
At Ensisheim, in France, archaeologists found a man buried around seven thousand years ago.
His skull had not one, but two of these holes.
And around the edges, new bone had grown back. One hole had closed over completely.
Bone only heals in someone who's alive. So he survived. Twice.
He's not alone. Healed trepanned skulls turn up in many parts of the ancient world.
Many patients lived on afterwards.
Why do it? Nobody is completely sure.
Maybe to treat a head injury, or bad headaches, or something people believed was trapped inside.
Either way, please don't try this at home.
Now let's meet a patient who carried his own first-aid kit.
In 1991, hikers in the Alps found a man frozen in the ice. He'd died about five thousand three hundred years ago.
Scientists call him Otzi, the Iceman.
And among his belongings were lumps of a fungus, threaded onto leather strips.
It's called birch polypore, and it contains natural chemicals that fight germs.
Inside Otzi's gut, scientists found the eggs of whipworm, a parasite that can cause tummy pain.
So some scientists think the fungus may have been his medicine.
We can't know for sure. But it would make sense.
Otzi also had sixty-one tattoos. Not pictures, just little lines and crosses.
Many sit over his lower back, knees and ankles, places where his joints were worn and may well have ached.
Some scientists think the tattoos may have been a kind of pain treatment.
Others aren't convinced. The debate is still going.
So, here's what getting sick might have looked like for Moss.
A bitter plant for his sore tummy. A green plant paste on his cut.
And if things got really bad, friends who brought him food, and kept him warm.
Of course, ancient medicine wasn't magic.
Lots of people still died from things we can treat easily today.
But remember that child in Borneo, thirty-one thousand years ago?
Someone made a brave, careful plan to save them. And then people looked after them, for years.
Maybe the oldest medicine wasn't a plant at all.
Maybe it was people refusing to leave anyone behind.
Follow for more of how ancient humans really lived.
